Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN)  -- A man accused of entering New York's LaGuardia Airport with a bag containing wires and batteries, sparking suspicion and leading to a large-scale evacuation, was ordered Saturday to undergo a psychiatric evaluation, a prosecutor said. LaGuardia Airport's Central Terminal is being treated as a crime scene. Scott McGann, 32, appeared in court after authorities said he walked into LaGuardia's Central Terminal Saturday morning with what was determined to be a fake bomb. The terminal was reopened after several hours. Queens District Attorney Richard A. Brown said McGann was charged with placing a false bomb or hazardous substance in the first degree; placing a false bomb or hazardous substance in a transportation facility; and making terrorist threats. McGann appeared in court Saturday, but his arraignment was postponed, Brown said. McGann is being held without bail. "The defendant is clearly a very troubled young man," Brown said. "As a result, the Court has directed that he be examined to determine whether he has the capacity to understand the proceedings against him and assist in his defense." Earlier, officials said McGann wouldn't speak to his lawyer or anyone else. His next court appearance is scheduled for Thursday. McGann allegedly arrived at a checkpoint in the terminal at about 4:50 a.m., carrying a backpack and refusing to answer security questions. Authorities said the officer at the checkpoint was informed that a suspicious package was attached to the bottom of McGann's backpack, and that McGann allegedly grabbed what appeared to be a trigger device with a red button connected to the backpack. McGann allegedly pressed the button several times before a Port Authority officer grabbed the trigger and the package away from him. The package turned out to be a device consisting of batteries, cylinders and electronic components that could have been used to make a bomb, Brown said, but the bomb squad found that it didn't not contain any explosives. McGann had a ticket on a United Airlines flight to Chicago and a seat on two other connecting flights with his final destination Oakland, California, according to a law enforcement official close to the investigation.  Watch passengers talk about the confusion » . McGann has three prior arrests in the New York area, the source told CNN. The most recent involved June charges of tampering with evidence and resisting arrest. He was also arrested twice in 2008, the source said. Port Authority spokesman John Kelly said McGann "was just acting crazy." The arresting officers described McGann to Kelly as "extremely disheveled and dirty," in a "near catatonic state" and "staring off into space," Kelly said. McGann had been homeless for at least a year. Authorities evacuated the terminal after 5:20 a.m., and allowed passengers back in to all areas except Concourse C by midmorning, Kelly said. The concourse was reopened shortly before 11 a.m., according to Federal Aviation Administration spokeswoman Holly Baker.  Watch the chaotic evacuation scene » . Authorities had stopped flights from taking off or landing at the airport, but by a little after 9 a.m., flights resumed, Baker said. Central Terminal is one of four terminals in the airport, which is in the borough of Queens. It is about eight miles from Manhattan. The incident disrupted travel plans for many passengers, and caused American Airlines to cancel 16 flights, said an airline spokesperson. American Eagle, Continental Airlines and Southwest also reported delays. iReport: Watch crowds start moving back into the terminal . CNN i-Reporter Jose Ojeda, 24, had been sitting on the tarmac on a plane headed to Chicago, Illinois, when the evacuation was ordered. "We were all ready to go," Ojeda, of Bronx, New York, said of his flight, which he said had been scheduled to leave at 6:10 a.m. "They didn't make any announcement other than, 'You need to evacuate,'" he said. "I thought it was standard procedure, but then once we got out of the plane, they kept pushing us back and back, out of the terminal out of the actual airport." CNN's Chuck Johnston, Aspen Steib, Ross Levitt, Laurie Segall and Susan Candiotti contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
**NEW YORK (CNN) —** A man accused of entering New York’s LaGuardia Airport with a bag containing wires and batteries—raising suspicions and prompting a large-scale evacuation—was ordered Saturday to undergo a psychiatric evaluation, a prosecutor said.

LaGuardia Airport’s Central Terminal was treated as a crime scene.

Scott McGann, 32, appeared in court after authorities said he entered the Central Terminal on Saturday morning carrying what was later determined to be a fake bomb. The terminal reopened several hours later.

Queens District Attorney Richard A. Brown said McGann was charged with placing a false bomb or hazardous substance in the first degree, placing a false bomb or hazardous substance in a transportation facility, and making terrorist threats.

McGann appeared in court Saturday, but his arraignment was postponed, Brown said. He is being held without bail.

“The defendant is clearly a very troubled young man,” Brown said. “As a result, the Court has directed that he be examined to determine whether he has the capacity to understand the proceedings against him and assist in his defense.”

Officials said earlier that McGann would not speak to his lawyer or anyone else. His next court appearance is scheduled for Thursday.

McGann allegedly arrived at a terminal checkpoint at about 4:50 a.m., carrying a backpack and refusing to answer security questions. Authorities said the officer at the checkpoint was informed that a suspicious package was attached to the bottom of McGann’s backpack. McGann then allegedly grabbed what appeared to be a trigger device with a red button connected to the backpack.

McGann allegedly pressed the button several times before a Port Authority officer seized the trigger and the package from him.

The package proved to be a device made up of batteries, cylinders, and electronic components that could have been used to build a bomb, Brown said. However, the bomb squad determined that it did not contain any explosives.

According to a law enforcement official close to the investigation, McGann had a ticket for a United Airlines flight to Chicago and seats on two connecting flights, with Oakland, California, as his final destination.

*Watch passengers discuss the confusion »*

McGann has three prior arrests in the New York area, the source told CNN. The most recent involved charges filed in June for tampering with evidence and resisting arrest. He was also arrested twice in 2008, the source said.

Port Authority spokesman John Kelly said McGann “was just acting crazy.” The arresting officers described McGann to Kelly as “extremely disheveled and dirty,” in a “near catatonic state,” and “staring off into space,” Kelly said.

McGann had been homeless for at least a year.

Authorities evacuated the terminal shortly after 5:20 a.m. and allowed passengers to return to all areas except Concourse C by midmorning, Kelly said. The concourse reopened shortly before 11 a.m., according to Federal Aviation Administration spokeswoman Holly Baker.

*Watch the chaotic evacuation scene »*

Authorities temporarily halted all takeoffs and landings at the airport, but flights resumed shortly after 9 a.m., Baker said.

The Central Terminal is one of four terminals at the airport, which is located in the borough of Queens, about eight miles from Manhattan.

The incident disrupted the travel plans of many passengers and prompted American Airlines to cancel 16 flights, an airline spokesperson said. American Eagle, Continental Airlines, and Southwest also reported delays.

*iReport: Watch crowds begin moving back into the terminal »*

CNN i-Reporter Jose Ojeda, 24, was sitting on the tarmac aboard a plane bound for Chicago, Illinois, when the evacuation was ordered.

“We were all ready to go,” Ojeda, of the Bronx, New York, said of his flight, which he said had been scheduled to depart at 6:10 a.m.

“They didn’t make any announcement other than, ‘You need to evacuate,’” he said. “I thought it was standard procedure, but then once we got out of the plane, they kept pushing us back and back, out of the terminal, out of the actual airport.”

CNN’s Chuck Johnston, Aspen Steib, Ross Levitt, Laurie Segall, and Susan Candiotti contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
NEW YORK (CNN) — A judge on Saturday ordered a psychiatric assessment for a man accused of bringing a backpack filled with wires, batteries and other components into New York’s LaGuardia Airport, prompting fears of a bomb and a major evacuation, according to a prosecutor.

Authorities treated LaGuardia’s Central Terminal as a crime scene after Scott McGann, 32, entered the building Saturday morning carrying what investigators later determined was a hoax explosive device. The terminal resumed operations several hours later.

Queens District Attorney Richard A. Brown said McGann faces charges of first-degree placement of a false bomb or hazardous substance, placement of a false bomb or hazardous substance in a transportation facility, and making terrorist threats.

Although McGann went before a judge Saturday, his formal arraignment was delayed, Brown said. He remains in custody without bail.

Brown described McGann as “clearly a very troubled young man.” He said the court had ordered an examination to establish whether McGann could understand the legal case against him and help with his own defense.

Officials earlier reported that McGann would not communicate with either his attorney or anyone else. He is expected to return to court Thursday.

Authorities allege that McGann approached a security checkpoint in the Central Terminal at approximately 4:50 a.m. with a backpack and declined to respond to security questions. The officer staffing the checkpoint was told that a suspicious object was fastened to the bottom of the bag.

McGann then allegedly took hold of what looked like a triggering mechanism—a device with a red button attached to the backpack—and pushed the button repeatedly. A Port Authority officer seized both the apparent trigger and the package from him.

Brown said the object contained batteries, cylinders and electronic parts that could potentially be used in constructing a bomb. However, a bomb squad inspection found no explosives inside.

A law enforcement official familiar with the investigation said McGann held a ticket for a United Airlines flight to Chicago, as well as reservations on two connecting flights that would ultimately take him to Oakland, California.

Passengers described the confusion caused by the incident.

The same source told CNN that McGann had previously been arrested three times in the New York area. His latest arrest involved charges filed in June for evidence tampering and resisting arrest. He was also taken into custody on two occasions in 2008.

Port Authority spokesman John Kelly said McGann “was just acting crazy.” According to Kelly, the officers who arrested him characterized him as “extremely disheveled and dirty,” said he appeared to be in a “near catatonic state,” and reported that he was “staring off into space.”

McGann had been without a home for at least a year.

The terminal was cleared sometime after 5:20 a.m., Kelly said. By the middle of the morning, travelers were permitted to return everywhere except Concourse C. Federal Aviation Administration spokeswoman Holly Baker said that concourse reopened shortly before 11 a.m.

The evacuation produced a chaotic scene. Officials temporarily suspended all arrivals and departures at LaGuardia, but flights began operating again shortly after 9 a.m., Baker said.

Located in Queens, roughly eight miles from Manhattan, the Central Terminal is one of LaGuardia Airport’s four terminals.

The disruption affected numerous travelers. An American Airlines representative said the carrier canceled 16 flights, while American Eagle, Continental Airlines and Southwest Airlines also experienced delays. Video submitted through CNN’s iReport showed crowds beginning to re-enter the terminal.

CNN i-Reporter Jose Ojeda, 24, was aboard a Chicago-bound aircraft sitting on the tarmac when authorities issued the evacuation order. Ojeda, who is from the Bronx in New York, said his flight had been scheduled to depart at 6:10 a.m. and that everyone had been prepared to leave.

“The only thing they announced was, ‘You need to evacuate,’” he said. Ojeda initially assumed it was a routine measure, but after passengers exited the aircraft, officials continued moving them farther away—first out of the terminal and then out of the airport itself.

CNN’s Chuck Johnston, Aspen Steib, Ross Levitt, Laurie Segall and Susan Candiotti contributed to the report.

The suspicious package was found to contain batteries, cylinders, wires, and other electronic components, but investigators determined that it contained no explosives.

McGann was charged with placing a false bomb in a transportation facility and making terrorist threats. He was ordered held without bail.

A man carrying what appeared to be an explosive device triggered a major security response and the evacuation of part of New York’s LaGuardia Airport. The object, assembled from batteries, wires, and other electronic components, initially raised fears that it might be a bomb.

Police and bomb-squad personnel secured the area while travelers and airport employees were moved to safety. After examining the device, investigators determined that it contained no explosives and was incapable of detonating. The affected terminal reopened several hours later once authorities concluded there was no continuing threat.

Prosecutors charged the man with offenses related to possession of a false bomb and making a terrorist threat. During the ensuing court proceedings, a judge ordered him to undergo a psychiatric evaluation. The assessment is intended to determine whether he is legally competent—that is, whether he understands the nature of the charges and court process and can meaningfully assist his attorney in preparing a defense.

Further proceedings will depend in part on the results of that evaluation.

# LaGuardia Airport Evacuated After Man Allegedly Activates Trigger Connected to Backpack

**NEW YORK —** Authorities evacuated part of LaGuardia Airport after a 32-year-old man experiencing homelessness allegedly pressed a trigger connected to a backpack containing wires and batteries, prompting fears that the bag could hold an explosive device.

According to preliminary accounts from law-enforcement officials, the man was inside the airport when he displayed or activated what appeared to be a trigger attached to the backpack. The visible electronic components immediately raised concern among airport personnel and travelers.

Officers moved people away from the area and established a security perimeter while bomb technicians examined the bag. The evacuation disrupted passenger movement as authorities restricted access and directed travelers to safer locations.

The presence of wires and batteries did not, by itself, establish that the backpack contained explosives. Such components can be used in an improvised device, however, and officials treated the situation as a potential bombing threat until specialists could determine whether the bag was capable of causing harm.

The man was detained, and investigators began working to establish what he intended to do, how the device was assembled and whether he had made any threats. Authorities had not immediately announced formal charges or released a complete inventory of the backpack’s contents.

No explosion was reported. Information about injuries, the duration of the evacuation and the effect on flights was not immediately available.

LaGuardia, one of the busiest airports serving New York City, maintains a large security presence, and reports of suspicious packages can lead to rapid evacuations and significant delays. Airport officials advised passengers to monitor flight information and follow instructions from police and airline personnel.

The incident remained under investigation, and officials cautioned that initial details could change as officers reviewed surveillance footage, interviewed witnesses and completed a forensic examination of the backpack.
